The relationships of Cyornis camarinensis have yet to be conclusively resolved but it is very similar to the Palawan Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis lemprieri) in structure and all plumages (10). For now, it is tentatively grouped within a subset of 15 unplaced Cyornis species in the most recent synthetic phylogeny of Muscicapidae (19). The fact that both Cyornis camarinensis and Cyornis lemprieri are Philippine endemics may make a sister relationship between these two seem especially likely, although Luzon and Palawan share few if any narrow endemics, and most modern global lists do not place them together in the linear sequence, Wolters being an exception (20). Given its similarity and former conspecificity, the species’ closest relative is almost certainly the Blue-breasted Blue Flycatcher (Cyornis herioti).

Together with Yellow-crowned Flowerpecker, with which it was formerly considered conspecific, Flame-crowned Flowerpecker resembles the Bicolored Flowerpecker (Dicaeum bicolor) in its bill shape (but this is even heavier in the present species) and in color pattern (although Bicolored Flowerpecker lacks the bright color patch). It also resembles the Cebu Flowerpecker (Dicaeum quadricolor), to which it and Bicolored Flowerpecker have been speculated to be closely related (5). Flame-crowned Flowerpecker and Yellow-crowned Flowerpecker together were confirmed, with strong support, to be sister to Bicolored Flowerpecker (among those taxa in the phylogeny, not including Cebu Flowerpecker), based on mtDNA sequence data and one nuclear intron, and to be members of the Dicaeum clade as opposed to the Prionochilus and Pachyglossa clades that contain most of the other thick-billed flowerpeckers (20, 21).

The most comprehensive phylogenetic systematic interrogation of Dacnis species was not able to sample the Scarlet-breasted Dacnis. Thus, molecular systematics has not been able to test the hypothesis that the Scarlet-breasted Dacnis is indeed a species of Dacnis (Burns et al. 2014). The Scarlet-breasted Dacnis is morphologically quite different from other species in the genus, and Burns (et al. 2014) regarded its placement as uncertain. Superficially its plumage resembles that of the Tit-like Dacnis (Xenodacnis parina), which is placed in Diglossinae (Burns et al. 2014). In addition, Storer (1970) doubted whether Dacnis berlepschi was closely related to other species of Dacnis, and Wolters (1975–1982) considered Xenodacnis parina and D. berlepschi closely related, placing both within the genus Xenodacnis. Following current taxonomy, the genus Dacnis includes the Scarlet-breasted Dacnis and 8 others species in the genus (Burns et al. 2016). Within Thraupidae (tanagers), Dacnis is placed in the subfamily Dacninae along with the Swallow Tanager (Tersina viridis) and Cyanerpes honeycreepers, though how these genera are related to each other remains unsupported (Burns et al. 2003, Burns et al. 2014).
